No soybean crushing facilities or ethanol plants were identified within either the 50- or 100-mile zones surrounding the selected airports. As a result, vegetable oils and associated byproducts are not locally available but could potentially be sourced from other regions if needed. Similarly, livestock operations were not observed in proximity to the selected airports, limiting access to manure or other animal-derived feedstocks in these areas. The most abundant biomass resources identified within both 50- and 100-mile radii were MSW and food waste. This is largely due to the airports being situated in or near densely populated urban areas, where waste generation is highest. Figure 6–Figure 13 illustrate the spatial distribution of biomass feedstocks across the broader region. As expected, there is a strong correlation between population density and the availability of MSW and yellow/brown grease, as these estimates were calculated on a per-capita basis. In contrast, forest residues show an inverse pattern—these resources are predominantly located outside of densely populated zones, with the highest concentrations observed in northern New Hampshire and Maine. Crop residues are more localized, primarily found in the agricultural zones of New York and New Jersey, and are distributed in a more dispersed pattern compared to urban-derived wastes. Trends in the distribution of sludge and animal fats were less apparent due to limited data resolution and the nature of the selected airport locations. However, some localized overlaps were observed in Massachusetts, particularly in the Boston and Springfield areas in the northeast and southwest parts of the state, respectively. Table 6.
